questions.q: In the default 1-token-1-vote model shown in this lesson's Tally screenshot, what determines a voter's power?
options: The number of tokens they hold plus whatever's been delegated to them
The number of proposals they've previously voted on
A fixed amount, identical for every address
How long ago they joined the protocol
questions.explain: voting_power(address) = balance(address) + sum(delegated_to(address)) -- the default model this lesson describes.

questions.q: Why is voting power measured at a snapshot block instead of read live when a vote is cast?
options: Snapshotting has no real security purpose -- it's purely for display
Because tokens can only be transferred once per block
To prevent a voter from borrowing tokens via a flash loan, voting, and repaying the loan within a single transaction
To let voters change their vote as many times as they want
questions.explain: Reading live voting power would let someone flash-loan tokens to temporarily inflate their power; a snapshot at proposal creation closes that hole.

questions.q: What does delegation give a delegate (like Bob in this lesson's example) the ability to do?
options: Transfer the delegator's tokens to any address
Cast votes with the delegator's voting weight -- without ever gaining the ability to move the delegator's tokens
Permanently take ownership of the delegator's tokens
Nothing -- delegation has no functional effect
questions.explain: Delegation (via a function like delegate()) hands off voting weight only. The delegate never gains custody or transfer rights over the underlying tokens.

questions.q: What does Aave's representative voting flow, shown in this lesson, let a participant do?
options: Automatically transfer their tokens to the DAO treasury
Bypass quorum requirements entirely
Vote twice on the same proposal
Choose a representative who can submit votes on their behalf on the voting network
questions.explain: The representative voting flow lets a governance participant delegate vote-casting to a chosen representative, without requiring the original holder to transact on every proposal.

questions.q: In the ERC20Votes-style delegation example, after Alice calls token.delegate(bob), what happens to Alice's 10,000 tokens?
options: They are transferred to Bob's wallet
They are locked in a smart contract permanently
They stay in Alice's wallet; only her voting weight is counted toward Bob
They are burned
questions.explain: Delegation is non-custodial: Alice's tokens never leave her wallet, but their voting weight counts toward Bob until she re-delegates.
